Counting principles

Product rule

∣A×B∣=∣A∣⋅∣B∣|A \times B| = |A|\cdot|B|∣A×B∣=∣A∣⋅∣B∣

Choices made one after another multiply.

Symbols: ∣A∣\lvert A\rvert∣A∣: the number of elements of AAA; A×BA \times BA×B: all pairs (one from AAA, one from BBB).

The idea

When a choice is made in stages — first one thing, then another — and every first choice can be combined with every second choice, the numbers of options multiply. The grid shows it: 3 columns × 4 rows = 12 points.

Worked example

3 shirts, 4 trousers and 2 pairs of shoes give 3⋅4⋅2=243\cdot 4\cdot 2 = 243⋅4⋅2=24 different outfits.

3 shirts and 4 trousers: 3⋅4=123\cdot4 = 123⋅4=12 outfits.

Sum rule

∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣|A \cup B| = |A| + |B|∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣(A∩B=∅)(A \cap B = \varnothing)(A∩B=∅)

Separate cases add.

Symbols: ∪\cup∪: union (either), ∩\cap∩: intersection (both), ∅\varnothing∅: the empty set.

The idea

When you choose one option from several groups that do not overlap — either this kind or that kind — the numbers add. Check that no option is in two groups; if one is, use inclusion–exclusion instead.

Worked example

A menu has 4 meat dishes and 3 fish dishes. Choosing one main course: 4+3=74 + 3 = 74+3=7 ways.

Go by one of 3 trains or one of 2 buses: 3+2=53 + 2 = 53+2=5 ways.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Complement

∣Aˉ∣=∣Ω∣−∣A∣|\bar A| = |\Omega| - |A|∣Aˉ∣=∣Ω∣−∣A∣

Count what you do not want and subtract.

Symbols: Ω\OmegaΩ: all the possible cases, Aˉ\bar AAˉ: those not in AAA.

The idea

“At least one” is often hard to count directly but easy to count the other way round: count everything, then subtract the cases with none at all.

Worked example

3-letter words with at least one A: all words 263=17 57626^3 = 17\,576263=17576, minus those with no A, 253=15 62525^3 = 15\,625253=15625: 195119511951.

4-digit PINs with some digit repeated: 104−10⋅9⋅8⋅7=496010^4 - 10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7 = 4960104−10⋅9⋅8⋅7=4960.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Restricted position first

3⋅5⋅4⋅3=1803\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3 = 1803⋅5⋅4⋅3=180

Fill the most restricted place first.

The idea

Fill boxes one by one and multiply the numbers of choices — but start with the box that has a condition (first digit not 0, last digit even…). If you start elsewhere, the number of choices for the restricted box depends on what was already used.

Worked example

3-digit numbers with distinct digits: the first digit has 9 choices (1–9), the second 9 (0 is back, one digit used), the third 8: 9⋅9⋅8=6489\cdot 9\cdot 8 = 6489⋅9⋅8=648.

Even 4-digit numbers with distinct digits from 1–6: last digit first (3 ways), then 5⋅4⋅35\cdot4\cdot35⋅4⋅3.

Arrangements

Permutations

n!=n(n−1)⋯2⋅1n! = n(n - 1)\cdots2\cdot1n!=n(n−1)⋯2⋅10!=10! = 10!=1

Symbols: n!n!n! (nnn factorial): the product 1⋅2⋯n1\cdot 2\cdots n1⋅2⋯n; the ways to order nnn different objects.

The idea

Lining up nnn different objects: nnn choices for the first place, n−1n - 1n−1 for the second, and so on down to 1. The product is n!n!n!, which grows extremely fast (10!=3 628 80010! = 3\,628\,80010!=3628800).

Worked example

4 people in a queue: 4!=244! = 244!=24 orders. Adding a fifth person multiplies by 5: 5!=1205! = 1205!=120.

5 books on a shelf: 5!=1205! = 1205!=120 orders.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

k out of n, in order

P(n,k)=n!(n−k)!P(n, k) = \frac{n!}{(n - k)!}P(n,k)=(n−k)!n!​

Symbols: nnn: objects available, kkk: how many you place in order.

The idea

Fill only kkk places: n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)n(n - 1)\cdots(n - k + 1)n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1), the first kkk factors of n!n!n!. Writing it as n!(n−k)!\tfrac{n!}{(n - k)!}(n−k)!n!​ just cancels the factors you did not use.

Worked example

A president and a secretary from 12 members: 12⋅11=13212\cdot 11 = 13212⋅11=132.

Gold, silver and bronze among 8 runners: 8⋅7⋅6=3368\cdot7\cdot6 = 3368⋅7⋅6=336.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

With repetition

nkn^knk

Symbols: nnn choices for each of kkk positions.

The idea

If the same element may be used again, every one of the kkk places has all nnn choices: n⋅n⋯n=nkn\cdot n\cdots n = n^kn⋅n⋯n=nk. Codes, passwords, sequences of coin tosses and dice rolls all work this way.

Worked example

Strings of 8 bits (0 or 1): 28=2562^8 = 25628=256 — that is why a byte has 256 values.

3-letter codes from 26 letters: 263=17 57626^3 = 17\,576263=17576.

Repeated letters

n!n1! n2!⋯nr!\frac{n!}{n_1!\,n_2!\cdots n_r!}n1​!n2​!⋯nr​!n!​

BANANA: 6!3! 2!=60\frac{6!}{3!\,2!} = 603!2!6!​=60.

Symbols: nnn: total letters; n1,…,nrn_1, \dots, n_rn1​,…,nr​: how many times each letter repeats.

The idea

Pretend all letters are different and count n!n!n! orders. Swapping two identical letters gives the same word, so every word was counted n1! n2!⋯n_1!\,n_2!\cdotsn1​!n2​!⋯ times: divide by them.

Worked example

LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice: 5!2! 2!=1204=30\tfrac{5!}{2!\,2!} = \tfrac{120}{4} = 302!2!5!​=4120​=30 words.

MISSISSIPPI: 11!4! 4! 2!=34 650\frac{11!}{4!\,4!\,2!} = 34\,6504!4!2!11!​=34650.

Round table

(n−1)!(n - 1)!(n−1)!

Bracelets that can be flipped: (n−1)!2\frac{(n - 1)!}{2}2(n−1)!​.

Symbols: nnn: the number of people; turning the table does not create a new arrangement.

The idea

Around a round table only the neighbours matter, not who sits “first”: turning everybody one seat gives the same seating. Fix one person’s seat and arrange the other n−1n - 1n−1: (n−1)!(n - 1)!(n−1)!.

Worked example

5 people at a round table: 4!=244! = 244!=24 seatings, not 5!=1205! = 1205!=120 — each seating appears 5 times among the 120, once per rotation.

6 people around a round table: 5!=1205! = 1205!=120.

Selections

Binomial coefficient

(nk)=n!k! (n−k)!\binom nk = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}(kn​)=k!(n−k)!n!​

Symbols: (nk)\binom nk(kn​) (“nnn choose kkk”): ways to pick kkk of nnn objects when order does not matter.

The idea

(nk)\binom nk(kn​) counts the ways to choose kkk items out of nnn when order does not matter: the ordered count n!(n−k)!\tfrac{n!}{(n - k)!}(n−k)!n!​ divided by the k!k!k! orders of each group. In practice, write kkk falling factors on top and k!k!k! below.

Worked example

Choose 2 of 5 friends to invite: (52)=5⋅42=10\binom52 = \tfrac{5\cdot 4}{2} = 10(25​)=25⋅4​=10 — the highlighted entry in row 5 of Pascal’s triangle.

A committee of 3 from 10 people: (103)=120\binom{10}{3} = 120(310​)=120.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Symmetry

(nk)=(nn−k)\binom nk = \binom n{n - k}(kn​)=(n−kn​)

The idea

Choosing the kkk items you take is the same as choosing the n−kn - kn−k you leave. So (nk)=(nn−k)\binom nk = \binom n{n - k}(kn​)=(n−kn​) — Pascal’s triangle is symmetric — and you always compute with the smaller of kkk and n−kn - kn−k.

Worked example

(2018)\binom{20}{18}(1820​) looks hard but equals (202)=20⋅192=190\binom{20}{2} = \tfrac{20\cdot 19}{2} = 190(220​)=220⋅19​=190.

Picking 8 of 10 players = picking the 2 who sit out: (108)=(102)=45\binom{10}{8} = \binom{10}{2} = 45(810​)=(210​)=45.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Pascal’s rule

(nk)=(n−1k−1)+(n−1k)\binom nk = \binom{n - 1}{k - 1} + \binom{n - 1}{k}(kn​)=(k−1n−1​)+(kn−1​)

The idea

Fix one special item. A group of kkk either contains it (choose the other k−1k - 1k−1 from the remaining n−1n - 1n−1) or not (choose all kkk from the remaining n−1n - 1n−1). In the triangle: each number is the sum of the two above it.

Worked example

(52)=(41)+(42)=4+6=10\binom52 = \binom41 + \binom42 = 4 + 6 = 10(25​)=(14​)+(24​)=4+6=10: the two yellow numbers in row 4 add to the yellow 10 below them.

Teams of 3 from 5, with Ana or without her: (42)+(43)=6+4=10\binom42 + \binom43 = 6 + 4 = 10(24​)+(34​)=6+4=10.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Sums

∑k=0n(nk)=2n\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk = 2^nk=0∑n​(kn​)=2n∑k(mk)(nr−k)=(m+nr)\sum_k\binom mk\binom n{r - k} = \binom{m + n}{r}k∑​(km​)(r−kn​)=(rm+n​)

The second is Vandermonde’s identity.

The idea

Adding a whole row of Pascal’s triangle counts every subset of an nnn-element set: each element is in or out, so 2n2^n2n. Vandermonde’s identity counts groups of rrr taken from two teams of mmm and nnn people by how many come from the first team.

Worked example

Row 5: 1+5+10+10+5+1=32=251 + 5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 32 = 2^51+5+10+10+5+1=32=25. A committee of 3 from 4 men and 5 women: (93)=84\binom93 = 84(39​)=84, which also equals (50)(43)+(51)(42)+(52)(41)+(53)(40)=4+30+40+10\binom50\binom43 + \binom51\binom42 + \binom52\binom41 + \binom53\binom40 = 4 + 30 + 40 + 10(05​)(34​)+(15​)(24​)+(25​)(14​)+(35​)(04​)=4+30+40+10.

Pizza toppings from 5: 25=322^5 = 3225=32 choices, the plain pizza included.

Committee with a chair

k(nk)=n(n−1k−1)k\binom nk = n\binom{n - 1}{k - 1}k(kn​)=n(k−1n−1​)

The idea

Count committees of kkk with one chair in two ways. Choose the committee, then its chair: k(nk)k\binom nkk(kn​). Or choose the chair first, then the other k−1k - 1k−1 members: n(n−1k−1)n\binom{n - 1}{k - 1}n(k−1n−1​). Both count the same thing, so they are equal.

Worked example

A committee of 3 with a chair from 10 people: 3(103)=3⋅120=3603\binom{10}{3} = 3\cdot 120 = 3603(310​)=3⋅120=360, or 10(92)=10⋅36=36010\binom92 = 10\cdot 36 = 36010(29​)=10⋅36=360.

3 of 10 with one as chair: 3(103)=10(92)=3603\binom{10}{3} = 10\binom92 = 3603(310​)=10(29​)=360.

With repetition

(n+k−1k)\binom{n + k - 1}{k}(kn+k−1​)

Symbols: Choose kkk items from nnn kinds, repeats allowed, order not important.

The idea

Choosing kkk items from nnn kinds, repeats allowed, order irrelevant: write kkk stars for the items and n−1n - 1n−1 bars between the kinds. Each choice is one arrangement of these n+k−1n + k - 1n+k−1 symbols, fixed by where the kkk stars go.

Worked example

3 pieces of fruit from 4 kinds (apple, pear, plum, fig): (63)=20\binom{6}{3} = 20(36​)=20. The picture ⋆⋆∣∣⋆∣\star\star\mid\mid\star\mid⋆⋆∣∣⋆∣ is two apples and one plum.

3 scoops from 5 flavours, repeats allowed: (73)=35\binom73 = 35(37​)=35.

Distributions and paths

Stars and bars

x1+⋯+xk=n, xi≥0:(n+k−1k−1)x_1 + \dots + x_k = n,\ x_i \ge 0:\quad \binom{n + k - 1}{k - 1}x1​+⋯+xk​=n, xi​≥0:(k−1n+k−1​)

Symbols: nnn identical objects into kkk boxes; xix_ixi​: how many go into box iii.

The idea

Share nnn identical objects among kkk people: line up nnn stars and k−1k - 1k−1 bars; person 1 gets the stars before the first bar, and so on. Choosing the positions of the k−1k - 1k−1 bars among n+k−1n + k - 1n+k−1 places gives the count.

Worked example

x1+x2+x3=5x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 5x1​+x2​+x3​=5 with xi≥0x_i \ge 0xi​≥0: 5 stars and 2 bars, (72)=21\binom72 = 21(27​)=21 solutions. ⋆⋆∣⋆∣⋆⋆\star\star\mid\star\mid\star\star⋆⋆∣⋆∣⋆⋆ is (2,1,2)(2, 1, 2)(2,1,2).

10 sweets for 4 children: (133)=286\binom{13}{3} = 286(313​)=286. Above: 3 + 2 + 4 + 1.

Positive solutions

xi≥1:(n−1k−1)x_i \ge 1:\quad \binom{n - 1}{k - 1}xi​≥1:(k−1n−1​)

The idea

If everybody must get at least one, put the nnn stars in a row and place the k−1k - 1k−1 bars in the n−1n - 1n−1 gaps between stars, at most one bar per gap. Equivalently, hand out one to each person first and share the remaining n−kn - kn−k freely.

Worked example

x1+x2+x3=7x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 7x1​+x2​+x3​=7 with xi≥1x_i \ge 1xi​≥1: choose 2 of the 6 gaps, (62)=15\binom62 = 15(26​)=15. Check: give 1 to each, then share 4 freely: (62)=15\binom{6}{2} = 15(26​)=15.

The same, but every child gets one: (93)=84\binom93 = 84(39​)=84.

Lattice paths

(0,0)→(m,n):(m+nm)(0, 0) \to (m, n):\quad \binom{m + n}{m}(0,0)→(m,n):(mm+n​)

Symbols: Paths of mmm steps right and nnn steps up; choose where the mmm right steps go.

The idea

A shortest path from (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) to (m,n)(m, n)(m,n) is a word of mmm R’s (right) and nnn U’s (up) in some order. Choosing which mmm of the m+nm + nm+n steps go right fixes the path.

Worked example

From (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) to (3,2)(3, 2)(3,2): 5 steps, 3 of them right, (53)=10\binom53 = 10(35​)=10 paths. The one drawn is RRURU.

(0,0)→(4,3)(0, 0) \to (4, 3)(0,0)→(4,3): choose where the 3 ↑ steps go among 7: (73)=35\binom73 = 35(37​)=35.

Catalan numbers

Cn=1n+1(2nn): 1,1,2,5,14,42,…C_n = \frac{1}{n + 1}\binom{2n}{n}: \ 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, \dotsCn​=n+11​(n2n​): 1,1,2,5,14,42,…

The idea

Many counting problems give 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, …: lattice paths from (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) to (n,n)(n, n)(n,n) that never go above the diagonal, ways to bracket a product, triangulations of a polygon. The formula takes all (2nn)\binom{2n}{n}(n2n​) paths and keeps the fraction 1n+1\tfrac{1}{n + 1}n+11​ of good ones.

Worked example

n=3n = 3n=3: 14(63)=204=5\tfrac14\binom63 = \tfrac{20}{4} = 541​(36​)=420​=5 paths to (3,3)(3, 3)(3,3) that stay on or below the diagonal — RRRUUU, RRURUU, RRUURU, RURRUU, RURURU.

3 pairs of brackets: ((())), (()()), (())(), ()(()), ()()() — C3=5C_3 = 5C3​=5.

Handshakes and diagonals

(n2)=n(n−1)2\binom n2 = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}(2n​)=2n(n−1)​(n2)−n=n(n−3)2\binom n2 - n = \frac{n(n - 3)}{2}(2n​)−n=2n(n−3)​

Symbols: nnn: the number of people (or vertices of the polygon).

The idea

Every handshake is a pair of people, so there are (n2)\binom n2(2n​). In a polygon with nnn vertices every pair of vertices is joined by a segment: nnn of them are sides, the rest are diagonals.

Worked example

10 people shake hands once each: (102)=45\binom{10}{2} = 45(210​)=45. An octagon has 8⋅52=20\tfrac{8\cdot 5}{2} = 2028⋅5​=20 diagonals.

10 people: (102)=45\binom{10}{2} = 45(210​)=45 handshakes; an octagon: 8⋅52=20\frac{8\cdot5}{2} = 2028⋅5​=20 diagonals.

Inclusion–exclusion

Two sets

∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣

The idea

Counting AAA and then BBB counts the elements of both twice — subtract them once. To count “neither”, subtract the union from the total.

Worked example

30 students, 18 play football, 15 basketball, 8 both: 18+15−8=2518 + 15 - 8 = 2518+15−8=25 play at least one, so 30−25=530 - 25 = 530−25=5 play neither.

18 play football, 15 basketball, 7 both: 18+15−7=2618 + 15 - 7 = 2618+15−7=26 play at least one.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Three sets

∣A∪B∪C∣=∑∣A∣−∑∣A∩B∣+∣A∩B∩C∣|A \cup B \cup C| = \sum|A| - \sum|A \cap B| + |A \cap B \cap C|∣A∪B∪C∣=∑∣A∣−∑∣A∩B∣+∣A∩B∩C∣

Symbols: ∑∣A∣\sum\lvert A\rvert∑∣A∣: add the three sizes; ∑∣A∩B∣\sum\lvert A \cap B\rvert∑∣A∩B∣: add the three pairwise intersections.

The idea

Add the three sets, subtract the three pairwise overlaps, then add back the triple overlap: the centre was added 3 times and removed 3 times, so it must be put back once.

Worked example

Integers 111–303030 divisible by 2, 3 or 5: 15+10+6−5−3−2+1=2215 + 10 + 6 - 5 - 3 - 2 + 1 = 2215+10+6−5−3−2+1=22.

Up to 100, divisible by 2, 3 or 5: 50+33+20−16−10−6+3=7450 + 33 + 20 - 16 - 10 - 6 + 3 = 7450+33+20−16−10−6+3=74.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Multiples up to N

#{n≤N:d∣n}=⌊Nd⌋\#\{n \le N : d \mid n\} = \left\lfloor\frac Nd\right\rfloor#{n≤N:d∣n}=⌊dN​⌋

Divisible by 2 or 3 up to 100: 50+33−16=6750 + 33 - 16 = 6750+33−16=67.

Symbols: ⌊ ⌋\lfloor\ \rfloor⌊ ⌋: round down to a whole number; d∣nd \mid nd∣n: ddd divides nnn.

The idea

The multiples of ddd up to NNN are d,2d,3d,…d, 2d, 3d, \dotsd,2d,3d,…, one every ddd numbers, so there are ⌊N/d⌋\lfloor N/d\rfloor⌊N/d⌋ of them (divide and drop the decimals). Multiples of both aaa and bbb are the multiples of their lcm.

Worked example

Multiples of 3 up to 20: ⌊20/3⌋=6\lfloor 20/3\rfloor = 6⌊20/3⌋=6 (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18). Multiples of 7 up to 100: ⌊100/7⌋=14\lfloor 100/7\rfloor = 14⌊100/7⌋=14.

Derangements

Dn=n!∑k=0n(−1)kk!≈n!eD_n = n!\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{(-1)^k}{k!} \approx \frac{n!}{e}Dn​=n!k=0∑n​k!(−1)k​≈en!​Dn=(n−1)(Dn−1+Dn−2)D_n = (n - 1)(D_{n-1} + D_{n-2})Dn​=(n−1)(Dn−1​+Dn−2​)

D1=0, D2=1, D3=2, D4=9, D5=44D_1 = 0,\ D_2 = 1,\ D_3 = 2,\ D_4 = 9,\ D_5 = 44D1​=0, D2​=1, D3​=2, D4​=9, D5​=44.

Symbols: DnD_nDn​: orderings of nnn objects in which none stays in its own place.

The idea

A derangement is an arrangement where nothing is in its own place — letters all in the wrong envelopes. Inclusion–exclusion over “item iii is in place” gives the alternating sum; it is about n!/en!/en!/e, so roughly 37% of all arrangements. The recursion is handy for small nnn: 0, 1, 2, 9, 44, 265.

Worked example

4 letters in 4 envelopes, all wrong: D4=24(1−1+12−16+124)=12−4+1=9D_4 = 24\left(1 - 1 + \tfrac12 - \tfrac16 + \tfrac1{24}\right) = 12 - 4 + 1 = 9D4​=24(1−1+21​−61​+241​)=12−4+1=9. Recursion check: 3(D3+D2)=3(2+1)=93(D_3 + D_2) = 3(2 + 1) = 93(D3​+D2​)=3(2+1)=9.

4 letters in 4 envelopes, none in its own: D4=9D_4 = 9D4​=9 (out of 4!=244! = 244!=24).

Pigeonhole principle

Basic form

n+1→n ⇒ ∃ i: ∣Bi∣≥2n + 1 \to n \ \Rightarrow\ \exists\,i:\ |B_i| \ge 2n+1→n ⇒ ∃i: ∣Bi​∣≥2

Put n + 1 objects into n boxes: some box gets at least two.

Symbols: BiB_iBi​: the boxes, ∣Bi∣\lvert B_i\rvert∣Bi​∣: how many objects box iii holds.

The idea

Put n+1n + 1n+1 objects into nnn boxes: some box gets at least two. It does not say which box — it only guarantees one exists. The art is choosing what the boxes are (months, remainders, colours).

Worked example

In any group of 13 people, two were born in the same month: 13 people, 12 months.

Among any 5 whole numbers, two leave the same remainder when divided by 4.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

General form

N→k ⇒ ∃ i: ∣Bi∣≥⌈Nk⌉N \to k \ \Rightarrow\ \exists\,i:\ |B_i| \ge \left\lceil\frac Nk\right\rceilN→k ⇒ ∃i: ∣Bi​∣≥⌈kN​⌉

13 people guarantee two with the same birth month; 25 guarantee three.

Symbols: NNN objects, kkk boxes; ⌈ ⌉\lceil\ \rceil⌈ ⌉: round up to a whole number.

The idea

If NNN objects go into kkk boxes, the average box holds N/kN/kN/k, and some box must hold at least the average — rounded up, because counts are whole numbers.

Worked example

100 people, 12 months: ⌈100/12⌉=⌈8.33⌉=9\lceil 100/12\rceil = \lceil 8.33\rceil = 9⌈100/12⌉=⌈8.33⌉=9, so some month has at least 9 birthdays.
